subcategory: California native vernal pool annual wildflower

planting.note: Scatter seed onto bare, exposed mud at the bottom of a seasonally flooded basin in fall; seed germinates underwater or in saturated mud once winter rains arrive.

directions: Toothed calicoflower is a low, mat-forming annual of Central Valley and foothill vernal pool bottoms that carpets drying mud in small two-lipped flowers, each petal marked with fine purple veining over a white-and-yellow throat. It is adapted to germinate while still submerged and then complete flowering and seed-set as the pool floor cracks and dries through late spring, so it belongs in the deepest, longest-ponding part of a constructed seasonal basin rather than a typical border bed. Because the whole plant disappears with the dry season, pair it with a companion that holds visual interest through summer once the display fades.

subcategory: California native vernal pool annual wildflower

planting.note: Direct sow onto bare mud at the lowest point of a seasonal basin in fall, the same way other Downingia species are established; it needs standing winter water followed by a hard spring dry-down.

directions: Endemic to vernal pools of the inner Central Valley and bay-area foothills between the Tehachapi Mountains and the San Francisco Bay, flatface calicoflower produces small, flattened violet-blue blooms that sit nearly against the mud rather than rising on an upright stem like its taller relatives. It thrives only where winter rain ponds for weeks at a time and then recedes completely, making it a good choice for the center of a hardpan or clay-lined basin that other calicoflowers also occupy. Avoid any summer watering of the site, since residual moisture after its natural dry-down window encourages rot rather than a second flush of bloom.

subcategory: California native vernal pool annual wildflower

planting.note: Broadcast seed into the deepest, standing-water zone of a seasonal basin in fall; unlike most pool annuals this species tolerates true submersion for weeks and flowers once water recedes.

directions: Smooth goldfields is one of the few vernal pool annuals that can grow rooted underwater for much of the winter, sending simple yellow daisy flowers up through shallow standing water or across the mud once it recedes. Its hairless, succulent stems and leaves distinguish it from the fuzzier upland Lasthenia species that colonize the drier pool rims, so it is best reserved for the lowest, most persistently flooded part of a constructed basin. It makes a strong late-season color echo alongside goldfields growing on the surrounding slopes, extending the yellow-flowered display after the drier-ground species have already finished.

subcategory: California native vernal pool grassland annual wildflower

planting.note: Direct sow in fall over bare, lightly raked soil on the moist grassy margins around a seasonal wet area; winter-spring rain triggers germination without any irrigation.

directions: Stalked popcornflower is named for the slender stalk, or stipe, that lifts each tiny nutlet above the stem, a small structural detail that separates it under a hand lens from the more common popcorn flower found across the same Central Valley vernal pool grasslands. Its small white, yellow-throated flowers cluster along coiling inflorescences on the gently sloped ground just above the longest-ponding pool bottoms. Use it to thicken a wildflower meadow planting around the margins of a seasonal wet area, where it reseeds reliably as long as the site stays free of summer irrigation.

subcategory: California native vernal pool annual-to-biennial wildflower

planting.note: Sow into the lower, longest-ponding floor of a seasonal basin in fall; the rosette overwinters underwater and does not send up its spiny flower heads until the pool has fully dried in summer.

directions: California button-celery, also called Jepson's coyote thistle, spends its first months as a submerged basal rosette of spiny, strap-like leaves before sending up low, branching stems tipped with small spine-wrapped flower heads once the pool bed is bone dry in midsummer. This late bloom timing fills a gap left by the spring-flowering vernal pool annuals, giving a seasonal wet garden color well after the showier calicoflowers and goldfields have finished. Plant it in the same persistently flooded basin floor as other true pool-bottom species, since it struggles wherever the site drains too quickly to hold winter water for an extended stretch.

subcategory: California native vernal pool margin annual wildflower

planting.note: Broadcast seed in fall over the damp grassy ground that rings a seasonal wet area; inoculating with rhizobium is unnecessary since the species nodulates readily with local soil bacteria.

directions: Whitetip clover forms dense, low clusters of rose-purple flower heads tipped crisply in white, growing along the damp upper margins of vernal pools and seasonally wet grassland from California north into the Pacific Northwest and intermountain West. Its tight basal rosette and clover-typical trifoliate leaves spread readily in disturbed, saturated soil, making it a useful nitrogen-fixing filler between showier pool-margin wildflowers in a rain garden planting. Let the stand self-sow and dry down naturally with the surrounding grassland rather than mowing or watering it through summer, since the plant completes its entire life cycle within the single wet season.

subcategory: California native vernal pool annual mint

planting.note: Sow into the drying floor of a seasonal basin in fall alongside other true pool-bottom species; the aromatic foliage and flowers only appear after the site has drained and begun to dry in late spring.

directions: Douglas' mesa mint is a strongly aromatic annual restricted to the drying beds of Central Valley and San Francisco Bay Area vernal pools, where its small, square stems carry whorls of pink-purple tubular flowers above narrow, pungent leaves. Crushing the foliage releases a sharp mint scent that helps separate it from the other low annuals sharing the same cracked-mud habitat. Reserve it for the deepest part of a constructed vernal pool feature that holds winter water for an extended period, since the plant will not flower on a site that dries out too early in spring.

subcategory: California native vernal pool annual wildflower

planting.note: Scatter fine seed over bare mud on the drying floor or lower margins of a seasonal basin in fall; the tiny seedlings need open, unshaded ground to establish.

directions: Slender woolly marbles forms tiny, ground-hugging gray-green mats covered in soft hairs, with each stem tip bearing a small round cluster of inconspicuous flowers that give the plant its common name. It is easy to overlook next to showier calicoflowers and goldfields, but it fills in bare mud patches on vernal pool floors and margins that would otherwise stay open, helping knit together a more complete seasonal wet-area planting. Because the whole plant is only an inch or two tall, place it where it will not be shaded out by taller pool-margin companions during its brief spring growing window.

subcategory: California native vernal pool annual wildflower

planting.note: Broadcast seed onto bare mud at the bottom of a seasonal basin in fall or very early winter; this is one of the earliest vernal pool species to germinate and finish its cycle, often flowering in late winter.

directions: Tiny mousetail is a minute, fast-cycling annual that gets its name from the slender, elongating seed receptacle that stretches above the small greenish flowers like a narrow tail. It is typically the first vernal pool species to germinate and finish flowering each year, often completing its entire cycle by mid-spring while other pool-bottom annuals are just beginning to bloom. Because it is so small and easy to lose among larger companions, scatter it thickly over open mud in the basin floor rather than mixing it into a crowded meadow planting, and expect it to vanish completely well before summer.
